paragraphs.source_en: The spiritual significance of mouflon and antelope in the Round Head art is also evident from their frequent association with the presumed ritual scenes with masked and decorated anthropomorphic figures, and also from some paintings where a direct relationship of humans and animals is apparent. A composition at Sefar represents a male anthropomorphic figure holding an enigmatic object in his left hand, slightly resembling a bow (Fig. 5-16). Around it and also under the figure there are small crosses–stars? The man is depicted with a false tail. His right hand is exaggeratedly long and it finishes in an antelope's head. The animal's head is thus directly united with the man and vice versa.

paragraphs.source_en: A different unity of man and antelope is depicted at Tan Zoumaitak (Fig. 5-17). A male anthropomorphic figure, perhaps dancing, has human form except for his legs. Instead of having human feet, he has antelope's hooves depicted in the same way as on antelope in the same shelter. Depictions of half-man half-animal, so abundant in the South African rock art (Lewis-Williams 2004), are extremely rare in the Round Head complex, and therianthropes, abundant in the neighbouring Bubaline engravings, are apparently nonexistent in the Round Head art.

paragraphs.source_en: It is not only the numerical predominance of mouflon and antelope over other animals indicating that these two animals were fundamental for the Round Head art and probably the culture. The unity of mouflon and antelope with the humans attested in the paintings, suggests that they belonged to the same spiritual world.
